title: ExecutionContext & ArgumentsHost: HTTP, WebSocket, and Microservice Abstraction
prerequisites: HTTP vs WebSocket vs RPC transports

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Imagine a universal power adapter that can plug into a standard wall socket (HTTP), a high-voltage machine (WebSockets), or a ship generator (Microservices). `ArgumentsHost` is that adapter: it lets your guards and error filters work identically no matter what kind of connection the user is using.
progressiveExplaining.junior: `ArgumentsHost` is an abstraction provided to filters, guards, and interceptors that gives access to the underlying protocol arguments. You use `host.switchToHttp()` (to get `req`, `res`), `host.switchToWs()` (to get `client`, `data`), or `host.switchToRpc()` (to get `data`, `context`). `ExecutionContext` extends `ArgumentsHost` by adding metadata about the current controller class (`context.getClass()`) and method handler (`context.getHandler()`).
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, `ArgumentsHost` decouples cross-cutting concerns (guards, exception filters, interceptors) from specific transport layers. A single `@Catch()` filter or `@Injectable()` guard can inspect `host.getType()` (`'http' | 'ws' | 'rpc' | 'graphql'`) and dynamically extract the appropriate protocol payload. `ExecutionContext` enables reflection-driven access control by pairing `context.getHandler()` with the `Reflector` service to read `@SetMetadata()` annotations.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: Under the hood, `ArgumentsHost` wraps an `args: any[]` array corresponding to the underlying transport driver. In HTTP (Express), `args = [req, res, next]`. In WebSockets, `args = [client, data]`. In Microservices, `args = [data, context]`. `switchToHttp()` returns an `HttpArgumentsHost` wrapper with helper methods `getRequest()` (`args[0]`) and `getResponse()` (`args[1]`), avoiding brittle array indexing.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the difference between `ArgumentsHost` and `ExecutionContext`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your precision with NestJS core interface hierarchies.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: `ArgumentsHost` provides access *only* to the underlying transport arguments (`switchToHttp()`, `switchToWs()`, `switchToRpc()`, `getArgs()`). It is passed to Exception Filters. `ExecutionContext` **extends `ArgumentsHost`** and adds metadata about the execution pipeline: `getClass()` (the Controller class constructor) and `getHandler()` (the route handler method reference). It is passed to Guards and Interceptors.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Exception Filters receive `ArgumentsHost`, not `ExecutionContext`, so they cannot call `context.getHandler()`.

interviewGotchas.question: How do you inspect custom metadata set on a controller method using `ExecutionContext` and `Reflector`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks knowledge of reflection and role-based access control.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Inject the `Reflector` service and call `reflector.get('roles', context.getHandler())` or `reflector.getAllAndOverride('roles', [context.getHandler(), context.getClass()])` to merge and override class-level metadata with method-level metadata.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Always pass `[context.getHandler(), context.getClass()]` to `getAllAndOverride` so method-level decorators take precedence over controller-level decorators.
